form: ɬe meʔmʔéw̓s te nk̓y̓ep eɬ x̣aʔx̣ʔéyqʷ nqəmmín - Mr. and Mrs. Coyote and their Magic Kettle wlwlmelst (Maurice Michell), Jonathan Janzen1 Kanaka Bar Indian Band Abstract: This paper is a back-translation of the “Mr. and Mrs. Coyote and their Magic Kettle” story (Stewart 1941). It has been translated back into the original nɬeʔkepmxcín by wlwlmelst (Maurice Michell) to the best of his ability and knowledge. Its purpose is to add to the growing body of written nɬeʔkepmxcín literature, educate on traditional knowledge, and further spark interest in nɬeʔkepmx research.

form: “Mr. and Mrs. Coyote and their Magic Kettle” is the first of a well-known series of stories published in English in “Meet Mr. Coyote” (Stewart 1941). This publication is a small booklet of ten nɬeʔképmx stories, with illustration by students of Noel Stewart at St. George's Indian Residential School in Lytton, B.C. It was published by the British Columbia Indian Arts and Welfare Society in 1941. The legends originate around the ƛ̓q̓əmcín (Lytton, B.C.) area. The storyteller and recorder of the original transcription of these stories is unknown, but the stories themselves are attributed to James Teit. wlwlmelst could find no written record of this story in the original nɬeʔkepmxcín, so he translated it back into his language based on the English translation given by the students of Stewart (1941). wlwlmelst took it upon himself to transcribe this story, relying on the spelling conventions set out by the Thompson River Salish Dictionary (Thompson & Thompson 1996). He shares his language freely for the benefit of those who seek to connect with this traditional story and its teachings. Our purposes for this publication is to bring further attention to the nɬeʔképmx language, and provide important resources for language learners. We want to gently remind readers that wlwlmelst puts considerable effort into his work. He transcribed and translated this story personally and was recorded reading it aloud with his younger brother nk̓y̓ep (Ernie Michell) who provides the English narration. His transcriptions were edited only when we were sure our changes would benefit understanding, and conform to the nɬeʔképmx orthographic standard.

wlwlmelst is one of the few remaining speakers of the Southern utémkt dialect of nɬeʔkepmxcín, which includes all communities on the Fraser River, South of Skuppah, from Siska through to Spuzzum. His way of presenting the language may differ from that of other fluent speakers. Some of the differences in language presented in this paper will be due to dialect variance, some might be idiosyncratic free variation in the language, and more than a few are likely due to errors in the analysis, and are the responsibility of Jonathan Janzen. Nevertheless, wlwlmelst’s words as presented are an accurate representation of the language that was passed to him by his ancestors.

form: Mr. and Mrs. Coyote and their Magic Kettle is a story that introduces the following nine stories in the published series (Stewart 1941). This story is broken down into four sections: exposition or scene setting, rising action, climax, and dénouement. This is the typical event structure of traditional nɬeʔképmx story-telling, according to wlwlmelst. The exposition gives the background to the story’s main characters: Mr. and Mrs. Coyote. It emphasizes their special status among the other animal people, and their special relationship to the Creator. The rising action section introduces the intrigue of the story: the magic basket. The climax of this story explains the importance and power of the magic basket as a source of provision, healing, and protection. Finally the dénouement concludes the story, and offers a conclusion for the whole series of ten stories: after thousands of years, Mr. and Mrs. Coyote return to the Creator, or ‘Father of Mysteries’, taking their magic kettle with them.

form: Long, long ago when the animal people lived in British Columbia, they were all very friendly together and looked loyally to Mr. and Mrs. Coyote as their leader. They were clever folk, so that when after many years mankind first appeared in their world, it was the animal people who taught these men how to build shelters against wind and rain. How to make fire for warmth and how to make stone tools.

form: Before Mr. and Mrs. Coyote left the sky world, the Father of Mysteries gave Mrs. Coyote this wonderful kettle made of coiled basket work. It could hold water and cook food. But of much greater importance it had the magic power to grant the wishes of the owner and to protect her from danger.
gloss: page 3, the English of the story as Stewart 1941 gives it, one paragraph

form: Who can be surprised at the care taken by Mrs. Coyote of the precious gift, for it possessed another amazing property. If by chance Mrs. Coyote was injured, a sweet herb or flower or fine shade tree instantly sprang up to heal the wound. And once, when by accident Mrs. Coyote was shot in one arm and lost much strength, at that exact moment a much needed stream began to flow on a far distant hillside, providing an ample supply of pure water for the thirsty folks who lived there.

form: So the animal people felt very sad when, after Mrs. Coyote had spent four thousand years among them, she decided to climb up the magic ladder down which she came to the earth, and return to the great Father of Mystery, taking with her this precious magic basket.

form: The following table defines all abbreviated glosses that appear in the interlinear analysis. They are organized alphabetically by morpheme, starting with the glottal stop, ʔ, to stay consistent with the Thompson & Thompson (1996) dictionary. Modern glossing conventions are used in the Gloss column, following research that has been ongoing since the 1990s, most notably UBC’s “nɬab”3. The gloss definitions that are derived from the Thompson & Thompson (1992) grammar are given in the T&T Gloss column. Direct quotes are referenced with the shortened form of this publication, (T&T 1992), followed by a page number.
